data.sourceTitle: Causes of the English Civil War
data.targetTitle: Causes of the English Civil War
data.sourcePassage:
The English Civil War did not break out because of one single argument. It grew from a combination of political, religious, economic and personal tensions that built up over many years.

Kings James I and Charles I both believed strongly in divine right, the idea that their authority came directly from God. This put them in conflict with Parliament, which believed it had important rights, especially over taxation. During his Personal Rule from 1629 to 1640, Charles I governed without Parliament, raising money through Ship Money, a tax extended to inland counties and collected in peacetime. Many people argued this was taxation without proper consent.

Religion made the conflict worse. Charles supported Archbishop Laud's church reforms, which many Puritans feared looked too close to Catholic practices. When Charles tried to impose a new prayer book on Scotland in 1637, rebellion broke out. This forced him to recall Parliament in 1640, giving MPs the opportunity to challenge his policies.

The relationship between king and Parliament became increasingly hostile. In January 1642, Charles tried to arrest five MPs, a move many saw as an attack on Parliament itself. Both sides began preparing for armed conflict, and war broke out in August 1642 when Charles raised his standard at Nottingham.

questions.question: What does 'divine right' mean?
options: The right of Parliament to approve all taxes
The belief that a monarch's authority came from God
The right of the Church to appoint bishops
The right of the army to remove a king
questions.modelAnswer: Divine right was the belief that a monarch's authority came directly from God and therefore could not be challenged by Parliament or the people.

questions.question: Why did Charles I's attempt to impose a prayer book on Scotland cause a crisis?
options: It made Scotland richer and more powerful than England
It led to a Scottish rebellion that forced Charles to recall Parliament
It caused France to declare war on England
It made the English army rebel against Charles
questions.modelAnswer: The attempt to impose a new prayer book on Scotland in 1637 triggered a rebellion, and Charles needed money to deal with the conflict, forcing him to recall Parliament in 1640.

questions.question: What was controversial about Ship Money?
options: It was used to fund a war against France
It was extended to inland counties and collected in peacetime without Parliament's consent
It was collected only in London and the south
It was a tax that Parliament had introduced against the king's wishes
questions.modelAnswer: Ship Money was controversial because Charles I extended it to inland counties and collected it in peacetime, which many argued was taxation without Parliament's consent.

questions.question: According to the passage, why was the Civil War the result of many causes rather than one?
options: Because Charles I was the only person responsible for events
Because Parliament deliberately planned a war from the start
Because political, religious, economic and personal tensions built up over many years
Because Scotland and France conspired to start the conflict
questions.modelAnswer: The passage explains that the Civil War grew from a combination of political, religious, economic and personal tensions that built up over many years, with no single cause being responsible alone.

data.sourceTitle: The Civil War, the Trial, and the Execution of Charles I
data.targetTitle: The Civil War, the Trial, and the Execution of Charles I
data.sourcePassage:
The English Civil War began in 1642 and involved England, Wales, Scotland and Ireland in a series of connected conflicts. Parliament's forces were strengthened in 1645 when the New Model Army was created. More professionally organised than earlier armies, it was promoted on ability rather than social status and had strong religious motivation. It proved decisive at the Battle of Naseby in 1645, destroying Charles I's main army. Charles surrendered in 1646.

However, Charles continued to negotiate with different groups while secretly trying to restart the conflict. This led to a Second Civil War in 1648. Many army leaders believed Charles could not be trusted. After Pride's Purge removed MPs who opposed the army's plans, a special court was established to try the king.

Charles I refused to recognise the court's authority, arguing that no court had the right to try a lawful king. He was found guilty and executed on 30 January 1649. His execution was shocking across Britain and Europe because kings were usually considered above ordinary courts.

The execution was significant because it challenged divine right monarchy and demonstrated that, in the view of Parliamentarian leaders, a king could be held accountable for harming his people. It abolished the monarchy temporarily and created the republic known as the Commonwealth. However, it did not create modern democracy, as political power remained limited to wealthy men.

questions.question: When was Charles I executed?
options: 30 January 1642
30 January 1649
30 January 1660
30 January 1689
questions.modelAnswer: Charles I was executed on 30 January 1649, after being found guilty by the special court established by Parliament.

questions.question: Why was the New Model Army created in 1645?
options: To help Charles I defeat Scotland
To create a more disciplined and professionally organised parliamentary force
To replace Parliament as the governing body of England
To enforce the Bill of Rights
questions.modelAnswer: The New Model Army was created in 1645 to give Parliament a more professionally organised and disciplined force, promoted on ability rather than social status.

questions.question: What was Pride's Purge?
options: The execution of Charles I in 1649
The removal of MPs who opposed the army's plan to try the king
The creation of the New Model Army
The dissolution of Parliament during the Personal Rule
questions.modelAnswer: Pride's Purge was the removal from Parliament of MPs who opposed the army's plans to put Charles I on trial, leaving only those willing to support the trial.

questions.question: Why was the execution of Charles I historically significant, according to the passage?
options: Because it created full modern democracy in England
Because it challenged the idea that a king was above the law and showed he could be held accountable
Because it ended all conflict in Britain and Ireland immediately
Because it gave women the right to vote in Parliament
questions.modelAnswer: The execution was significant because it challenged divine right monarchy and showed that a king could be held accountable by his political opponents, even though it did not create modern democracy.

data.sourceTitle: The Restoration and the Glorious Revolution
data.targetTitle: The Restoration and the Glorious Revolution
data.sourcePassage:
After the execution of Charles I, England became a republic called the Commonwealth. The Commonwealth faced serious problems: many people still supported the monarchy, Parliament was divided, and the army held great power. In 1653, Oliver Cromwell became Lord Protector, beginning the Protectorate period. Cromwell was a complex figure who supported some Protestant religious toleration and maintained order, but he also relied heavily on military power. His campaigns in Ireland were especially controversial.

Cromwell died in 1658. His son Richard lacked political support and resigned within months. With no stable government in place, many people wanted a return to the familiarity of monarchy. In 1660, Charles II was invited back to rule. This was the Restoration. The monarchy, House of Lords and Church of England were all restored, though kings now had to be more careful about working with Parliament.

In 1685, Charles II was followed by his Catholic brother James II. James's attempts to increase royal power and promote policies favouring Catholics alarmed many Protestant politicians. In 1688, leading figures invited the Protestant William of Orange to intervene. James II fled to France. William III and Mary II became joint monarchs in what became known as the Glorious Revolution.

In 1689, the Bill of Rights confirmed that the monarch could not suspend laws without Parliament, that taxation required parliamentary consent, and that Parliament should meet regularly. This marked a significant shift of power from the Crown to Parliament, though England was still far from a modern democracy.

questions.question: What was the Restoration?
options: The execution of Charles I in 1649
The return of the monarchy in 1660 when Charles II became king
The creation of the Commonwealth after the Civil War
The passing of the Bill of Rights in 1689
questions.modelAnswer: The Restoration was the return of the monarchy in 1660, when Charles II was invited back to rule England after years of republican government.

questions.question: Why did the Glorious Revolution happen in 1688?
options: Because Charles II wanted to retire from being king
Because James II was too Protestant for many people
Because James II's Catholic beliefs and attempts to increase royal power alarmed Protestant politicians
Because Parliament decided a Dutch king would be better for trade
questions.modelAnswer: The Glorious Revolution happened because James II was Catholic and attempted to increase royal power, alarming many Protestant politicians who then invited William of Orange to intervene.

questions.question: What did the Bill of Rights of 1689 establish?
options: That the monarch had unlimited power to govern without Parliament
That taxation required parliamentary consent and Parliament should meet regularly
That only Catholics could sit in Parliament
That Oliver Cromwell's descendants should rule England
questions.modelAnswer: The Bill of Rights established that taxation required parliamentary consent, that the monarch could not suspend laws without Parliament, and that Parliament should meet regularly.

questions.question: According to the passage, why is the term 'Glorious Revolution' considered debatable?
options: Because William III was not really Protestant
Because the events were entirely bloodless and therefore not a true revolution
Because the name can hide the fact that violence did occur in Scotland and Ireland
Because James II agreed to leave peacefully
questions.modelAnswer: The passage notes the Glorious Revolution is a contested name because it can make the events seem simpler and bloodless, even though violence occurred in Scotland and Ireland during this period.
